items.stem: The lanthanoids and actinoids form which block?
items.answer: f-block
items.markingKey: f-block. They fill 4f and 5f sublevels.

items.stem: Why does potassium appear in period 4 rather than period 3?
options: It has four neutrons more than sodium.
Its outermost electron enters the 4s sublevel, which fills before 3d.
items.answer: Its outermost electron enters the 4s sublevel, which fills before 3d.
items.markingKey: D. [Ar] 4s¹.

items.stem: Which outer-shell configuration is shared by the elements of group 17?
items.answer: ns² np⁵
items.markingKey: C. Group 17 → ns² np⁵.

items.stem: An element has the ground-state configuration [He] 2s² 2p³. Where is it in the periodic table?
items.answer: period 2, group 15
items.markingKey: A. Highest occupied level n = 2 → period 2; outer configuration → group 15 (p-block): nitrogen.

items.stem: In which block of the periodic table is bromine (Z = 35) found?
items.answer: p-block
items.markingKey: A. bromine: [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p⁵; highest-energy electron in a p sublevel.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "The periodic table is the most important organising principle in chemistry."
items.answer: It is a central organising tool, but it summarises underlying quantum principles rather than replacing them.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: predicts properties and reactivity from position; summarises electron configurations and periodic trends; predicted undiscovered elements (Mendeleev, gallium and germanium). Arguments against: position does not fully predict properties (e.g. hydrogen, anomalous first members of groups); other principles (conservation of energy, equilibrium) are equally fundamental; f-block placement and group 3 membership are still debated. Supported judgement: It is a central organising tool, but it summarises underlying quantum principles rather than replacing them.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "metalloid".
items.answer: An element with properties intermediate between those of metals and non-metals, such as boron, silicon, germanium, arsenic and tellurium
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: an element with properties intermediate between those of metals and non-metals, such as boron, silicon, germanium, arsenic and tellurium. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why elements in the same group have similar chemical properties.
items.answer: They have the same number of electrons in their outer shell (same outer configuration), and chemical reactions involve the outer electrons, so they react in similar ways.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They have the same number of electrons in their outer shell (same outer configuration), and chemical reactions involve the outer electrons, so they react in similar ways. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between the p-block and the s-block.
items.answer: In the s-block the outermost electron enters an s sublevel (groups 1, 2); in the p-block it enters a p sublevel (groups 13–18).
items.markingKey: In the s-block the outermost electron enters an s sublevel (groups 1, 2); in the p-block it enters a p sublevel (groups 13–18). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Elena writes: "Hydrogen is an alkali metal because it is in group 1." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Hydrogen has one valence electron (1s¹) but is a non-metal that forms H₂ molecules; it is often placed separately because its properties do not match group 1.
items.markingKey: Hydrogen has one valence electron (1s¹) but is a non-metal that forms H₂ molecules; it is often placed separately because its properties do not match group 1. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: State the outer-shell configuration shared by all elements in group 16.
items.answer: ns² np⁴
items.markingKey: ns² np⁴

items.stem: An atom of an element contains 35 electrons. Deduce the period, group and block of the element.
items.answer: [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p⁵: period 4, group 17, p-block
items.markingKey: Configuration [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p⁵ (1); period 4 and group 17 (1); p-block (1).

items.stem:
Diego analysed a lime fertiliser containing calcium oxide. A 0.320 g sample was dissolved in 25.00 cm³ of 1.000 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid (an excess). The solution was made up to 100.0 cm³, and 20.00 cm³ portions were titrated with 0.200 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide. The mean titre was 14.62 cm³.

(a) Calculate the amount, in mol, of HCl remaining in the 100.0 cm³ solution. [2]
(b) Determine the amount of CaO in the sample and its percentage purity. [3]
(c) Suggest a suitable indicator for the titration and state the colour change. [1]
(d) Explain why a back titration is used rather than titrating the oxide directly with acid. [2]
items.answer: (a) 0.0146 mol (b) 0.00519 mol; 91.0 % (c) phenolphthalein: colourless to pink (strong acid–strong base) (d) Calcium oxide is a sparingly soluble solid, so it reacts slowly and its end point would be hard to detect directly.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] n(NaOH) = 0.200 × 0.01462 = 0.00292 mol (M1); × 5 = 0.0146 mol (A1). (b) [3] n(HCl) reacted = 0.0250 − 0.0146 = 0.0104 mol (M1); n(CaO) = half = 0.00519 mol (M1); purity = 0.291/0.320 × 100 = 91.0 % (A1). (c) [1] indicator and colour change (1). (d) [2] Insoluble / slow-reacting solid (1); end point unclear in direct titration (1).

items.stem: Element Q has 33 electrons. (a) Write its full electron configuration. (b) Deduce its period, group and block. (c) Predict, with a reason, whether its oxide is acidic or basic. (d) Identify one other element with similar chemical properties.
items.answer: (a) 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p³. (b) period 4, group 15, p-block (arsenic). (c) acidic – non-metal/metalloid oxide. (d) phosphorus (or N, Sb) – same ns² np³ outer configuration.
items.markingKey: (a) 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p³. (b) period 4, group 15, p-block (arsenic). (c) acidic – non-metal/metalloid oxide. (d) phosphorus (or N, Sb) – same ns² np³ outer configuration.

items.stem: Which element has the most exothermic first electron affinity?
items.answer: chlorine
items.markingKey: chlorine. Cl −349 kJ mol⁻¹; F is smaller and suffers more electron repulsion.

items.stem: Explain the difference between an anion of the same element and a cation.
items.answer: Cations are smaller than their atoms (fewer electrons, often fewer shells); anions are larger (extra electron–electron repulsion, same nuclear charge).
items.markingKey: Cations are smaller than their atoms (fewer electrons, often fewer shells); anions are larger (extra electron–electron repulsion, same nuclear charge). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why atomic radius decreases across a period.
items.answer: Nuclear charge increases by one each element while electrons are added to the same main level, so shielding barely increases; the greater effective nuclear charge pulls the outer electrons closer. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Nuclear charge increases by one each element while electrons are added to the same main level, so shielding barely increases; the greater effective nuclear charge pulls the outer electrons closer. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: The first ionisation energy of calcium is 590 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the maximum wavelength of electromagnetic radiation, in nm, that could ionise a single gaseous calcium atom.
items.answer: 203 nm

items.stem: Predict, with a reason, whether rubidium or strontium has the larger atomic radius.
items.answer: Rubidium: same period, but Sr has one more proton with similar shielding, so its electrons are held closer.
items.markingKey: Rubidium: same period, but Sr has one more proton with similar shielding, so its electrons are held closer.

items.stem: Which of the elements aluminium, phosphorus, sulfur and calcium has the lowest electronegativity?
items.answer: calcium
items.markingKey: A. Pauling values: Al 1.6, P 2.2, Ca 1.0, S 2.6. Electronegativity increases across a period and decreases down a group.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Electronegativity is a less useful idea than ionisation energy because it cannot be measured directly."
items.answer: Both are useful: IE is more rigorous, but electronegativity is the more practical tool for predicting bonding.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: IE is a measured, well-defined quantity; electronegativity values depend on the scale used (Pauling, Mulliken). Arguments against: electronegativity predicts bond polarity and bond type, which IE does not; it underpins the bonding triangle and explains reactivity patterns. Supported judgement: Both are useful: IE is more rigorous, but electronegativity is the more practical tool for predicting bonding.

items.stem:
Lars analysed a zinc oxide cream base containing zinc oxide. A 0.493 g sample was dissolved in 25.00 cm³ of 1.000 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid (an excess). The solution was made up to 250.0 cm³, and 50.00 cm³ portions were titrated with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide. The mean titre was 28.22 cm³.

(a) Calculate the amount, in mol, of HCl remaining in the 250.0 cm³ solution. [2]
(b) Determine the amount of ZnO in the sample and its percentage purity. [3]
(c) State one assumption made in this calculation. [1]
(d) Explain why a back titration is used rather than titrating the oxide directly with acid. [2]
items.answer: (a) 0.0141 mol (b) 0.00545 mol; 89.9 % (c) The impurities do not react with hydrochloric acid. (d) Zinc oxide is a sparingly soluble solid, so it reacts slowly and its end point would be hard to detect directly.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] n(NaOH) = 0.100 × 0.02822 = 0.00282 mol (M1); × 5 = 0.0141 mol (A1). (b) [3] n(HCl) reacted = 0.0250 − 0.0141 = 0.0109 mol (M1); n(ZnO) = half = 0.00545 mol (M1); purity = 0.443/0.493 × 100 = 89.9 % (A1). (c) [1] Impurities unreactive with acid (1). (d) [2] Insoluble / slow-reacting solid (1); end point unclear in direct titration (1).

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "shielding".
items.answer: The reduction in attraction between the nucleus and outer electrons caused by repulsion from inner electrons
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the reduction in attraction between the nucleus and outer electrons caused by repulsion from inner electrons. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The minimum energy required to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms in their ground state"?
items.answer: first ionisation energy
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of first ionisation energy.

items.stem: Which statement explains why electronegativity increases across period 2?
options: Nuclear charge increases while the bonding electrons stay in the same shell.
items.answer: Nuclear charge increases while the bonding electrons stay in the same shell.
items.markingKey: D. Higher effective nuclear charge.

items.stem: "Electronegativity is measured in kJ mol⁻¹." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Electronegativity is a relative scale without units (Pauling scale); electron affinity and ionisation energy have units of kJ mol⁻¹.
items.markingKey: Electronegativity is a relative scale without units (Pauling scale); electron affinity and ionisation energy have units of kJ mol⁻¹. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Calculate the longest wavelength of light (in nm) able to remove the outer electron from a gaseous atom of rubidium, given that its first ionisation energy is 403 kJ mol⁻¹.
items.answer: 297 nm

items.stem: Which of fluorine, sodium, aluminium and potassium has the largest atomic radius?
items.answer: potassium
items.markingKey: C. Atomic radii / pm (data booklet): K 200, F 60, Al 124, Na 160. Radius decreases across a period and increases down a group.

items.stem: The atomic radius of aluminium is 124 pm and the ionic radius of Al³⁺ is 54 pm. Explain the difference.
items.answer: aluminium atom is larger: the cation has lost its outer shell, and the same nuclear charge now attracts fewer electrons more strongly.
items.markingKey: Correct comparison (1); the cation has lost its outer shell, and the same nuclear charge now attracts fewer electrons more strongly (1–2).

items.stem: Which of carbon, oxygen, phosphorus and bromine has the most exothermic first electron affinity?
items.answer: bromine
items.markingKey: A. First electron affinities / kJ mol⁻¹: Br −325, O −141, C −122, P −72.

items.stem: The first ionisation energies (kJ mol⁻¹) of period 3 are Na 496, Mg 738, Al 578, Si 787, P 1012, S 1000, Cl 1251, Ar 1521. (a) Describe the general trend and explain it. (b) Explain the decrease from Mg to Al. (c) Explain the decrease from P to S. (d) Predict, with a reason, the value for K relative to Na.
items.answer: (a) increases: increasing nuclear charge, same shell, similar shielding. (b) Al 3p electron is higher in energy and shielded by 3s². (c) S has a paired 3p electron; repulsion makes it easier to remove. (d) lower (419): 4s electron further away and more shielded.
items.markingKey: (a) increases: increasing nuclear charge, same shell, similar shielding. (b) Al 3p electron is higher in energy and shielded by 3s². (c) S has a paired 3p electron; repulsion makes it easier to remove. (d) lower (419): 4s electron further away and more shielded.

items.stem:
The atomic radii (pm) of some elements are shown.

element | atomic radius / pm
F | 60
Cl | ?
Br | 117
I | 136

(a) Estimate the atomic radius of chlorine. (b) Explain the trend shown in the table. (c) Predict, with a reason, how the first ionisation energies of these elements vary. (d) Suggest why ionic radii, rather than atomic radii, are used to explain the lattice enthalpies of their compounds.
items.answer: (a) between 60 and 117 pm (actual 100 pm); (b) radius increases down the group: more occupied shells, outer electrons further from the nucleus, more shielding; (c) IE decreases down the group.
items.markingKey: (a) value between 60 and 117 pm (A1). (b) increases down the group: more occupied shells, outer electrons further from the nucleus, more shielding (R1 R1). (c) IE decreases – outer electron less strongly attracted (R1). (d) in ionic compounds the ions, not atoms, are present; ionic radius sets the distance between charges (R1).

items.stem: Define the term "basic oxide".
items.answer: A metal oxide that reacts with acids to form a salt and water; soluble ones form alkaline solutions
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a metal oxide that reacts with acids to form a salt and water; soluble ones form alkaline solutions. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: How does calcium carbonate neutralise acid rain in lakes?
options: CaCO₃ reacts with H⁺ ions to form Ca²⁺, water and carbon dioxide.
It absorbs SO₂ from the air above the lake.
It forms a protective layer on the water.
items.answer: CaCO₃ reacts with H⁺ ions to form Ca²⁺, water and carbon dioxide.
items.markingKey: A. CaCO₃ + 2H⁺ → Ca²⁺ + H₂O + CO₂.

items.stem: Explain the difference between sodium oxide and phosphorus(V) oxide.
items.answer: Na₂O is ionic and basic, forming NaOH(aq) (pH 14); P₄O₁₀ is molecular covalent and acidic, forming H₃PO₄(aq) (pH ~2).
items.markingKey: Na₂O is ionic and basic, forming NaOH(aq) (pH 14); P₄O₁₀ is molecular covalent and acidic, forming H₃PO₄(aq) (pH ~2). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Ana writes: "Aluminium oxide is acidic because aluminium is in group 13." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Al₂O₃ is amphoteric: it reacts with both acids and bases.
items.markingKey: Al₂O₃ is amphoteric: it reacts with both acids and bases. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Write a balanced equation, with state symbols, for the reaction of sodium oxide with water and state whether the solution formed is acidic or alkaline.
items.answer: Na₂O(s) + H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq); alkaline
items.markingKey: Correct formulae (1); balanced (1). Na₂O(s) + H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq); alkaline

items.stem: The oxides of period 3 elements range from Na₂O to SO₃. (a) Describe the change in bonding and structure across the period. (b) Write equations for the reactions of Na₂O and SO₃ with water and state the approximate pH of each solution. (c) Explain why Al₂O₃ is described as amphoteric, with equations.
items.answer: (a) giant ionic (Na₂O, MgO, Al₂O₃) → giant covalent (SiO₂) → simple molecular (P₄O₁₀, SO₃). (b) Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH, pH 13–14; SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄, pH 0–1. (c) Al₂O₃ + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂O; Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH + 3H₂O → 2NaAl(OH)₄.
items.markingKey: (a) giant ionic (Na₂O, MgO, Al₂O₃) → giant covalent (SiO₂) → simple molecular (P₄O₁₀, SO₃). (b) Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH, pH 13–14; SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄, pH 0–1. (c) Al₂O₃ + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂O; Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH + 3H₂O → 2NaAl(OH)₄.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "acid deposition"?
options: An element that has an incomplete d sublevel in its atom or in one of its common ions
A vertical column of the periodic table containing elements with the same outer-shell electron configuration
The process by which acidic substances (from SO₂ and NOx) leave the atmosphere as wet (rain, snow) or dry deposits
The region of the periodic table (groups 3–12) in which the highest-energy electron occupies a d sublevel
items.answer: The process by which acidic substances (from SO₂ and NOx) leave the atmosphere as wet (rain, snow) or dry deposits
items.markingKey: C. "acid deposition" is the process by which acidic substances (from SO₂ and NOx) leave the atmosphere as wet (rain, snow) or dry deposits.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the oxides of the metals on the left of period 3 are basic.
items.answer: They are ionic and contain the oxide ion, O²⁻, which accepts protons (O²⁻ + H₂O → 2OH⁻; O²⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂O).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They are ionic and contain the oxide ion, O²⁻, which accepts protons (O²⁻ + H₂O → 2OH⁻; O²⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂O). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Which change in bonding occurs across the period 3 oxides?
items.answer: ionic to covalent
items.markingKey: C. Electronegativity difference with O decreases.

items.stem: "All oxides dissolve in water to give acidic or alkaline solutions." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Some oxides (Al₂O₃, SiO₂) are insoluble and give neutral water; their acid/base character is shown by their reactions with acids and bases.
items.markingKey: Some oxides (Al₂O₃, SiO₂) are insoluble and give neutral water; their acid/base character is shown by their reactions with acids and bases. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: How would SO₂ be classified?
items.answer: acidic
items.markingKey: D. SO₂: simple molecular covalent; acidic.

items.stem: Unpolluted rain has a pH of about 5.6. Rain collected near a coal-fired power station outside Melbourne had a pH of 4.6. Calculate how many times greater [H⁺] is in the polluted rain.
"Reducing sulfur emissions has solved the problem of acid deposition." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Major progress has been made, but NOx emissions and global variation mean the problem is reduced, not solved.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: flue-gas desulfurisation and low-sulfur fuels have cut SO₂ emissions sharply in Europe and North America; rain pH in many regions has recovered. Arguments against: NOx from vehicles and agriculture remain significant; emissions are rising in some industrialising regions; damaged soils and lakes recover slowly. Supported judgement: Major progress has been made, but NOx emissions and global variation mean the problem is reduced, not solved. Markbands (6 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem: "Ocean acidification is a more serious long-term threat than acid rain." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Acid rain is a more local and more controllable problem; ocean acidification is global and harder to reverse, so in the long term it is the more serious one.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: affects all oceans globally and is directly linked to rising CO₂; harms shell- and coral-forming organisms and marine food chains; very slow to reverse. Arguments against: acid rain has caused severe local damage to forests, lakes and buildings; acid rain is still a problem in some industrial regions. Supported judgement: Acid rain is a more local and more controllable problem; ocean acidification is global and harder to reverse, so in the long term it is the more serious one. Markbands (12 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The charge an atom would have if all its bonds were ionic; shown with a sign before the number, e.g. +3"?
items.answer: oxidation state
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of oxidation state.

items.stem: A student claims: "Zinc is a transition element because it is in the d-block." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Zinc has a full 3d¹⁰ sublevel in both the atom and its only ion Zn²⁺, so it does not meet the definition of a transition element.
items.markingKey: Zinc has a full 3d¹⁰ sublevel in both the atom and its only ion Zn²⁺, so it does not meet the definition of a transition element. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between a paramagnetic substance and a diamagnetic substance.
items.answer: Paramagnetic substances have unpaired electrons and are attracted into a magnetic field; diamagnetic substances have all electrons paired and are weakly repelled.
items.markingKey: Paramagnetic substances have unpaired electrons and are attracted into a magnetic field; diamagnetic substances have all electrons paired and are weakly repelled. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: For the Cu⁺ ion: (a) write its electron configuration; (b) state the number of unpaired electrons; (c) predict whether its aqueous complexes are coloured and whether they are paramagnetic.
items.answer: (a) [Ar] 3d¹⁰; (b) 0; (c) colourless, diamagnetic
items.markingKey: (a) [Ar] 3d¹⁰ – 4s removed first (1). (b) 0 (1). (c) colourless because 3d⁰ or 3d¹⁰ allows no d–d transitions (1); diamagnetic (1).

items.stem: A solution of a transition metal complex absorbs light most strongly at 480 nm. Calculate the energy difference between the split d orbitals in kJ mol⁻¹.
items.answer: 249 kJ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: C. E = hc/λ = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸ / 480 × 10⁻⁹ = 4.14 × 10⁻¹⁹ J per ion (M1); × 6.02 × 10²³ / 1000 = 249 kJ mol⁻¹ (A1). The solution appears approximately orange (complementary colour).

items.stem: A student prepares the complex ion [CoCl₄]²⁻, which is blue in solution. (a) Deduce the oxidation state of Co and write its electron configuration. (b) State the coordination number and the type of bond between the ligand and the metal. (c) Explain the origin of the colour. (d) Predict, with a reason, whether the complex is paramagnetic.
items.answer: (a) +2; [Ar] 3d⁷. (b) 4; coordination (dative covalent) bonds. (c) d–d transitions in split 3d orbitals; complementary colour seen. (d) paramagnetic (3 unpaired)
items.markingKey: (a) +2 (A1); [Ar] 3d⁷ (A1). (b) 4 (A1); ligand donates a lone pair (A1). (c) ligands split d orbitals; visible light absorbed promotes an electron; transmitted complementary colour (R1 R1). (d) 3 unpaired electrons → paramagnetic (R1).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "ligand"?
options: The process by which acidic substances (from SO₂ and NOx) leave the atmosphere as wet (rain, snow) or dry deposits
The net positive charge experienced by an outer electron: the nuclear charge minus the shielding by inner electrons
A molecule or negative ion with a lone pair of electrons that forms a coordination bond to a central metal ion
Able to react both as an acid and as a base, e.g. aluminium oxide
items.answer: A molecule or negative ion with a lone pair of electrons that forms a coordination bond to a central metal ion
items.markingKey: C. "ligand" is a molecule or negative ion with a lone pair of electrons that forms a coordination bond to a central metal ion.

items.stem: Why does iron form both Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺ ions?
options: The 4s and 3d electrons are close in energy, so either two or three can be lost.
Iron is in group 2 and group 3.
items.answer: The 4s and 3d electrons are close in energy, so either two or three can be lost.
items.markingKey: A. Similar energies of 3d and 4s.

items.stem: Explain why transition elements show variable oxidation states.
items.answer: The 3d and 4s electrons have similar energies, so different numbers of them can be lost (or used in bonding) without a very large jump in ionisation energy.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The 3d and 4s electrons have similar energies, so different numbers of them can be lost (or used in bonding) without a very large jump in ionisation energy. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: What is the oxidation state of nickel in the complex ion [Ni(H₂O)₆]²⁺?
items.markingKey: A. Ligand charges (H₂O) and overall charge of the complex give Ni = +2.

items.stem: Name a ligand that can form two coordination bonds to a metal ion.
items.answer: ethane-1,2-diamine (or ethanedioate) – a bidentate ligand
items.markingKey: ethane-1,2-diamine (or ethanedioate) – a bidentate ligand

items.stem: "Transition metals are essential to modern industrial chemistry." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: They are central to many key processes, but sustainability and toxicity concerns are driving the search for alternatives and recycling.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: catalysts: Fe (Haber), V₂O₅ (Contact), Ni (hydrogenation), Pt/Pd/Rh (catalytic converters); structural metals and alloys (steel, titanium); pigments and electronics. Arguments against: many are scarce, expensive or toxic (Cr(VI), Ni, Co); mining causes environmental damage; enzymes and organocatalysts can replace some uses. Supported judgement: They are central to many key processes, but sustainability and toxicity concerns are driving the search for alternatives and recycling. items.stem: Iron(III) chloride solution is yellow-brown and is paramagnetic. (a) Write the electron configuration of Fe³⁺. (b) Explain why the solution is coloured. (c) Explain why it is paramagnetic. (d) Suggest why a solution of Zn²⁺ ions is colourless and diamagnetic.
items.answer: (a) [Ar] 3d⁵. (b) water ligands split the 3d orbitals; visible light of energy matching the splitting is absorbed; complementary colour transmitted. (c) five unpaired 3d electrons. (d) Zn²⁺ is 3d¹⁰: no d–d transitions possible and all electrons paired.
items.markingKey: (a) [Ar] 3d⁵. (b) water ligands split the 3d orbitals; visible light of energy matching the splitting is absorbed; complementary colour transmitted. (c) five unpaired 3d electrons. (d) Zn²⁺ is 3d¹⁰: no d–d transitions possible and all electrons paired.

items.stem: Which element has the highest electronegativity?
items.answer: fluorine
items.markingKey: D. F = 4.0 on the Pauling scale.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A vertical column of the periodic table containing elements with the same outer-shell electron configuration"?
items.answer: group
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of group.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The process by which acidic substances (from SO₂ and NOx) leave the atmosphere as wet (rain, snow) or dry deposits"?
items.answer: acid deposition
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of acid deposition.

items.stem: "Copper sulfate solution is blue because it emits blue light." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: It absorbs light in the red-orange region (d–d transition) and transmits the complementary blue light.
items.markingKey: It absorbs light in the red-orange region (d–d transition) and transmits the complementary blue light. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Yusuf writes: "Negative ions are smaller than their atoms because they have extra electrons pulling inwards." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Electrons do not pull inwards; the extra electron increases repulsion while the nuclear charge is unchanged, so the anion is larger.
items.markingKey: Electrons do not pull inwards; the extra electron increases repulsion while the nuclear charge is unchanged, so the anion is larger. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between the p-block and the s-block.
items.answer: In the s-block the outermost electron enters an s sublevel (groups 1, 2); in the p-block it enters a p sublevel (groups 13–18).
items.markingKey: In the s-block the outermost electron enters an s sublevel (groups 1, 2); in the p-block it enters a p sublevel (groups 13–18). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between a basic oxide and an acidic oxide.
items.answer: A basic oxide (usually ionic, metal) reacts with acids and forms OH⁻ in water; an acidic oxide (usually covalent, non-metal) reacts with bases and forms H⁺/H₃O⁺ in water.
items.markingKey: A basic oxide (usually ionic, metal) reacts with acids and forms OH⁻ in water; an acidic oxide (usually covalent, non-metal) reacts with bases and forms H⁺/H₃O⁺ in water. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain how a ligand forms a bond to a transition metal ion.
items.answer: The ligand donates a lone pair of electrons into an empty orbital of the metal ion, forming a coordination (dative covalent) bond.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The ligand donates a lone pair of electrons into an empty orbital of the metal ion, forming a coordination (dative covalent) bond. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why a sodium ion is smaller than a sodium atom.
items.answer: Na⁺ has lost its 3s electron, so it has one fewer occupied main level, and the 11 protons now attract only 10 electrons more strongly.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Na⁺ has lost its 3s electron, so it has one fewer occupied main level, and the 11 protons now attract only 10 electrons more strongly. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Which element has chemical properties most similar to those of the element with atomic number 17?
items.answer: fluorine
items.markingKey: A. Z = 17 is chlorine (group 17); fluorine is in the same group with the same outer configuration.

items.stem: The pH of rain in Toronto fell from 5.6 to 4.3 over several decades. By what factor did the hydrogen ion concentration increase?
How many unpaired electrons are there in a gaseous Cr²⁺ ion?
items.markingKey: C. Cr²⁺: [Ar] 3d⁴ → 4 unpaired electrons (Hund’s rule).

items.stem: The ions O²⁻, Na⁺, Al³⁺ and N³⁻ are isoelectronic. Which has the largest radius?
items.answer: N³⁻
items.markingKey: B. Same number of electrons; O²⁻ has 8 protons, Na⁺ has 11 protons, Al³⁺ has 13 protons, N³⁻ has 7 protons. More protons → smaller ion.

items.stem: In which block of the periodic table is fluorine (Z = 9) found?
items.answer: p-block
items.markingKey: A. fluorine: [He] 2s² 2p⁵; highest-energy electron in a p sublevel.

items.stem: Calculate the volume, in cm³, of 1.00 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid needed to react exactly with 2.43 g of magnesium oxide.
items.answer: 121 cm³

items.stem: What is the oxidation state of oxygen in H₂O₂?
items.markingKey: A. O = −2 (−1 in peroxides), H = +1, K = +1; the sum equals the overall charge of H₂O₂, so O = −1.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Effective nuclear charge alone explains all periodic trends."
items.answer: It is the key idea across a period but must be combined with distance, shielding and sublevel structure.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: explains decrease in radius and increase in IE and electronegativity across a period; combined with distance it explains group trends. Arguments against: distance and shielding must be considered down a group; sublevel effects (2p vs 2s, paired electrons) cause anomalies in IE; electron–electron repulsion explains electron affinity anomalies (F vs Cl). Supported judgement: It is the key idea across a period but must be combined with distance, shielding and sublevel structure.

items.stem: "Mendeleev deserves more credit for the periodic table than any later chemist." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Mendeleev’s predictive table was a decisive step, but the modern table rests on later work on atomic number and electron structure.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: left gaps and predicted properties of undiscovered elements (eka-silicon = germanium); reordered elements (Te/I) by properties rather than strictly by mass. Arguments against: Moseley showed atomic number, not mass, is the ordering principle; quantum theory later explained why the pattern exists; others (Meyer, Newlands) produced similar arrangements. Supported judgement: Mendeleev’s predictive table was a decisive step, but the modern table rests on later work on atomic number and electron structure. Markbands (6 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Ocean acidification is a more serious long-term threat than acid rain."
items.answer: Acid rain is a more local and more controllable problem; ocean acidification is global and harder to reverse, so in the long term it is the more serious one.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: affects all oceans globally and is directly linked to rising CO₂; harms shell- and coral-forming organisms and marine food chains; very slow to reverse. Arguments against: acid rain has caused severe local damage to forests, lakes and buildings; acid rain is still a problem in some industrial regions. Supported judgement: Acid rain is a more local and more controllable problem; ocean acidification is global and harder to reverse, so in the long term it is the more serious one. Markbands (6 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem: "Transition metals are essential to modern industrial chemistry." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: They are central to many key processes, but sustainability and toxicity concerns are driving the search for alternatives and recycling.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: catalysts: Fe (Haber), V₂O₅ (Contact), Ni (hydrogenation), Pt/Pd/Rh (catalytic converters); structural metals and alloys (steel, titanium); pigments and electronics. Arguments against: many are scarce, expensive or toxic (Cr(VI), Ni, Co); mining causes environmental damage; enzymes and organocatalysts can replace some uses. Supported judgement: They are central to many key processes, but sustainability and toxicity concerns are driving the search for alternatives and recycling. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "first ionisation energy"?
options: Having the same number of electrons (and electron configuration), e.g. O²⁻, F⁻, Na⁺ and Mg²⁺
The net positive charge experienced by an outer electron: the nuclear charge minus the shielding by inner electrons
The process by which acidic substances (from SO₂ and NOx) leave the atmosphere as wet (rain, snow) or dry deposits
The minimum energy required to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms in their ground state
items.answer: The minimum energy required to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms in their ground state
items.markingKey: D. "first ionisation energy" is the minimum energy required to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms in their ground state.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "s-block"?
options: Having the same number of electrons (and electron configuration), e.g. O²⁻, F⁻, Na⁺ and Mg²⁺
The region of the periodic table (groups 1 and 2, plus He) in which the highest-energy electron occupies an s sublevel
The decrease in the pH of the oceans caused by the dissolving of atmospheric carbon dioxide to form carbonic acid
The enthalpy change when one mole of electrons is added to one mole of gaseous atoms to form one mole of gaseous 1− ions
items.answer: The region of the periodic table (groups 1 and 2, plus He) in which the highest-energy electron occupies an s sublevel
items.markingKey: B. "s-block" is the region of the periodic table (groups 1 and 2, plus He) in which the highest-energy electron occupies an s sublevel.

items.stem: Which gas is the main cause of natural acidity in rain water (pH ≈ 5.6)?
items.answer: carbon dioxide
items.markingKey: C. CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃.

items.stem: Why is Zn²⁺(aq) colourless?
options: Water is not a ligand for zinc.
Its 3d sublevel is full, so no d–d electron transitions can occur.
It has no d electrons at all.
items.answer: Its 3d sublevel is full, so no d–d electron transitions can occur.
items.markingKey: C. 3d¹⁰.

items.stem: Distinguish between nuclear charge and effective nuclear charge.
items.answer: Nuclear charge is the total number of protons; effective nuclear charge is what an outer electron actually feels after shielding by inner electrons.
items.markingKey: Nuclear charge is the total number of protons; effective nuclear charge is what an outer electron actually feels after shielding by inner electrons. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why the elements in period 2 are the first to show the full s and p sublevel pattern.
items.answer: Level n = 2 contains a 2s and three 2p orbitals, holding up to 8 electrons, so period 2 contains 8 elements from Li (2s¹) to Ne (2s² 2p⁶).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Level n = 2 contains a 2s and three 2p orbitals, holding up to 8 electrons, so period 2 contains 8 elements from Li (2s¹) to Ne (2s² 2p⁶). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why aluminium oxide is described as amphoteric.
items.answer: It reacts with acids (e.g. HCl, forming Al³⁺ salts) and with strong bases (NaOH, forming aluminate ions, Al(OH)₄⁻), so it behaves as both a base and an acid.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It reacts with acids (e.g. HCl, forming Al³⁺ salts) and with strong bases (NaOH, forming aluminate ions, Al(OH)₄⁻), so it behaves as both a base and an acid. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "When iron forms Fe²⁺, the electrons are removed from the 3d sublevel first." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The 4s electrons are lost first: Fe [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s² → Fe²⁺ [Ar] 3d⁶.
items.markingKey: The 4s electrons are lost first: Fe [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s² → Fe²⁺ [Ar] 3d⁶. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Why is the first electron affinity of most elements exothermic?
options: The added electron is attracted by the nucleus of the neutral atom.
Energy is needed to overcome repulsion.
The ion formed is always a noble gas.
items.answer: The added electron is attracted by the nucleus of the neutral atom.
items.markingKey: A. Attraction > repulsion for X(g) + e⁻.

items.stem: Where in the periodic table is the element whose atoms have the configuration [Ne] 3s² 3p⁵?
items.answer: period 3, group 17
items.markingKey: C. Highest occupied level n = 3 → period 3; outer configuration → group 17 (p-block): chlorine.

items.stem: Calculate the volume, in cm³, of 0.250 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid needed to react exactly with 1.66 g of sodium oxide.
items.answer: 214 cm³

items.stem: What is the coordination number of Ag in [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺?
items.markingKey: A. 2 coordination bonds from the ligands (NH₃).

items.stem: The first ionisation energy of lithium is 520 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the maximum wavelength of electromagnetic radiation, in nm, that could ionise a single gaseous lithium atom.
items.answer: 230 nm

items.stem: Write the condensed electron configuration of vanadium (Z = 23) and use it to state its period, group and block.
items.answer: [Ar] 3d³ 4s²: period 4, group 5, d-block
items.markingKey: Configuration [Ar] 3d³ 4s² (1); period 4 and group 5 (1); d-block (1).

items.stem: Equal amounts of Na₂O, P₄O₁₀, SO₃ and Cl₂O₇ are each added to separate beakers of water. Which beaker has the highest pH?
items.answer: Na₂O
items.markingKey: A. Approximate pH: Na₂O 14, P₄O₁₀ 2, SO₃ 1, Cl₂O₇ 1 (insoluble oxides leave water at about 7).

items.stem: A solution of a transition metal complex absorbs light most strongly at 500 nm. Calculate the energy difference between the split d orbitals in kJ mol⁻¹.
items.answer: 239 kJ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: E = hc/λ = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸ / 500 × 10⁻⁹ = 3.98 × 10⁻¹⁹ J per ion (M1); × 6.02 × 10²³ / 1000 = 239 kJ mol⁻¹ (A1). The solution appears approximately red (complementary colour).

items.stem:
The atomic radii (pm) of some elements are shown.

element | atomic radius / pm
Li | 130
Na | 160
K | 200
Rb | ?
Cs | 238

(a) Estimate the atomic radius of rubidium. (b) Explain the trend shown in the table. (c) Predict, with a reason, how the first ionisation energies of these elements vary. (d) Suggest why ionic radii, rather than atomic radii, are used to explain the lattice enthalpies of their compounds.
items.answer: (a) between 200 and 238 pm (actual 215 pm); (b) radius increases down the group: more occupied shells, outer electrons further from the nucleus, more shielding; (c) IE decreases down the group.
items.markingKey: (a) value between 200 and 238 pm (A1). (b) increases down the group: more occupied shells, outer electrons further from the nucleus, more shielding (R1 R1). (c) IE decreases – outer electron less strongly attracted (R1). (d) in ionic compounds the ions, not atoms, are present; ionic radius sets the distance between charges (R1).

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "The periodic table is the most important organising principle in chemistry."
items.answer: It is a central organising tool, but it summarises underlying quantum principles rather than replacing them.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: predicts properties and reactivity from position; summarises electron configurations and periodic trends; predicted undiscovered elements (Mendeleev, gallium and germanium). Arguments against: position does not fully predict properties (e.g. hydrogen, anomalous first members of groups); other principles (conservation of energy, equilibrium) are equally fundamental; f-block placement and group 3 membership are still debated. Supported judgement: It is a central organising tool, but it summarises underlying quantum principles rather than replacing them. Markbands (6 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem: "Reducing sulfur emissions has solved the problem of acid deposition." Discuss.
items.answer: Major progress has been made, but NOx emissions and global variation mean the problem is reduced, not solved.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: flue-gas desulfurisation and low-sulfur fuels have cut SO₂ emissions sharply in Europe and North America; rain pH in many regions has recovered. Arguments against: NOx from vehicles and agriculture remain significant; emissions are rising in some industrialising regions; damaged soils and lakes recover slowly. Supported judgement: Major progress has been made, but NOx emissions and global variation mean the problem is reduced, not solved. Markbands (6 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem: A student prepares the complex ion [Fe(SCN)(H₂O)₅]²⁺, which is blood red in solution. (a) Deduce the oxidation state of Fe and write its electron configuration. (b) State the coordination number and the type of bond between the ligand and the metal. (c) Explain the origin of the colour. (d) Predict, with a reason, whether the complex is paramagnetic.
items.answer: (a) +3; [Ar] 3d⁵. (b) 6; coordination (dative covalent) bonds. (c) d–d transitions in split 3d orbitals; complementary colour seen. (d) paramagnetic (5 unpaired)
items.markingKey: (a) +3 (A1); [Ar] 3d⁵ (A1). (b) 6 (A1); ligand donates a lone pair (A1). (c) ligands split d orbitals; visible light absorbed promotes an electron; transmitted complementary colour (R1 R1). (d) 5 unpaired electrons → paramagnetic (R1).
